title: Weight shard endianness regression investigation
summary: During a staged rollout of model-v2 to production canaries, a subset of inference hosts began returning degraded generations and increased token misalignment due to incorrectly interpreted weight shard byte order. Root cause traced to a build pipeline change that produced shards with an implicit endianness dependent on the builder host; some serving nodes assumed little-endian decoding and produced subtle numerical drift. This doc captures detection, timeline, mitigations taken, root cause analysis, and short-term and long-term corrective actions.
content:
Background:

On 2024-11-14 we started a progressive rollout of model-v2 (quantized 8-bit, sharded) using the normal staged rollout policy: canary=10% (10 hosts across two regions), then ramp to 50%, then full roll. The model artifacts are produced by the release pipeline that shards and serializes weights into per-GPU binary blobs. Previously we relied on the host platform and our loader to implicitly agree on endianness; no explicit endianness flag had been encoded into the artifact header.

What happened (high level):
- At 2024-11-14T19:21 UTC the first canary started returning outputs with 2–5x higher perplexity on our internal eval prompts and odd token alignment (repeats and off-by-one truncations).
- Monitoring alert (generation-quality-regression) triggered at 19:28 UTC after canary quality fell below threshold.
- Latency and infrastructure metrics were nominal; CPU/GPU utilization and OOMs were absent. The failure surface pointed to numerical/behavioral regression rather than resource exhaustion.
- By 20:05 UTC we identified a correlation: only nodes running the new container built on host-builder-3 (an Ubuntu 22.04 builder image) exhibited the regression. Other canaries (built on builder-1 and builder-2) were fine.

Detection details and evidence:
- Per-route eval hooks flagged an increase in token repetition and decreased BLEU/ROUGE-like ranking on internal eval suite.
- KV cache hit/miss patterns were similar across canaries, so cache logic was unlikely.
- Low-level float checks: running quick consistency checker on the loaded first-layer weights on the affected node showed bytewise differences compared to the canonical S3 stored copy when interpreted as little-endian floats vs big-endian floats; when reinterpreted with swapped endianness the values matched expected ranges.
- Checksum mismatches: our existing SHA256 checksums matched the artifact file bytes stored in S3, but the artifact serialization step could produce the same byte sequence regardless of endianness handling; the loader's reinterpretation mattered.
- Application logs contained warnings from the runtime: "float_cast_warning: exponent bits appear out-of-range" (non-fatal) on affected nodes, which had previously been suppressed as noisy but were important here.

Immediate mitigation timeline:
- 19:32 UTC: Canary ramp paused (automated by deployment policy) when the first regression alert fired.
- 19:45 UTC: On-call SREs attached to canary hosts and ran quick diagnostics (float re-interpretation, strided dot-product checks).
- 20:10 UTC: Identified builder host correlation and isolated affected hosts (4/10 canaries across region-us-west-2).
- 20:30 UTC: Rolled the affected canary hosts back to previous model-v1 artifact (safe known-good). This rollback restored generation quality to baseline within two evaluation windows.
- 21:05 UTC: Full rollback of the staged rollout (hold) until further investigation.

Root cause analysis (technical):
- The release pipeline step "shard-serialize" was updated in PR-879 to use a new binary serializer for speed. The serializer writes raw float bytes from the build host memory into shard files without normalizing endianness. On most builder hosts (builder-1, builder-2) this produced little-endian shards; builder-3, used for nightly builds, produced big-endian-ordered bytes in a specific container configuration due to a changed compiler flag and a cross-compile library that emitted different byte ordering for the host's runtime memory view.
- The serving runtime loader expects little-endian-ordered IEEE-754 32-bit floats when reconstructing weights and did not check or normalize endianness at load-time. When confronted with big-endian bytes the loader interpreted them incorrectly leading to subtle numeric perturbations that manifested as degraded generation quality.
- Artifact signing/manifest included only file-level SHA256 but no explicit schema/version/endianness metadata. Because the on-disk bytes matched S3 objects and the checksum matched, existing safety checks passed.

Contributing factors:
- Lack of a canonical, portable serialization format in the artifact spec (endianness not enforced/recorded).
- New serializer added for performance without compatibility tests across builder variants.
- Runtime was optimized to avoid per-shard byte-swapping for performance; assumption of homogeneous build environment hardened over time.
- Float-cast warnings in logs were not treated as actionable; they gave early signals but were noisy in other contexts and had been deprioritized.

Why this was subtle:
- The bytes were "valid" numeric encodings; they simply mapped to different floating values when interpreted with the wrong order. No crash, no OOM, no checksum failure — behavioral issue only detectable via quality checks.

Post-incident mitigations (short-term taken within 48h):
- Added immediate pre-deploy artifact endianness check in the release pipeline: a small canonical float pattern (magic array) is serialized to the shard header; the loader verifies and rejects artifacts with mismatched endianness. (Deployed 2024-11-15 03:00 UTC).
- Rebuilt and re-staged model-v2 artifacts using a normalized serializer that explicitly writes little-endian IEEE-754 floats regardless of builder host. New artifacts stored under s3://redwood-artifacts/models/2024-11-15/model-v2-normalized/ (PR-882).
- Re-enabled stricter runtime checks in canaries to treat float-cast-warning as fatal during staged rollouts for the next 7 days.
- Expanded canary diversity to exercise at least three distinct builder images and two OS families during validation.

Longer-term actions (owners & timelines):
- Action 1: Revise artifact schema to include explicit fields: serialization-version, endianness, float-format, and a per-shard sample checksum. Owner: eng-platform (Ravi Singh). ETA: 2024-12-05.
- Action 2: Replace custom fast serializer with portable serialization library (or add deterministic endianness normalization) and add unit tests that exercise all supported builder images. Owner: eng-build (Liam Chen). ETA: 2024-11-30.
- Action 3: Add binary-level portability tests into CI: build artifacts on builder variants and run a runtime verification job that loads shards in a sandboxed container and runs numeric sanity checks. Owner: eng-qa (Olivia Park). ETA: 2024-12-10.
- Action 4: Update runtime loader to detect and autodetect endianness mismatch and perform a one-time fast byte-swap during load when necessary, with telemetry emitting swap events. Owner: serving-runtime (Aisha Moreno). ETA: 2024-12-01.
- Action 5: Update deployment policy: during staged rollouts, require generation-quality smoke tests to pass on at least one host built with each builder image variant. Owner: eng-sre (Maya Gupta). ETA: 2024-12-03.
- Action 6: Audit logs and alerting: convert "float_cast_warning" into a structured metric used by the quality-regression detector. Owner: observability (TBD). ETA: 2024-11-29.

Lessons learned and recommendations:
- Assume heterogeneity across builders and explicitly encode portability guarantees in artifact formats.
- Behavioral regressions (quality) can be the only signal for subtle numeric corruption — binary checksums are necessary but insufficient.
- Small diagnostic headers (magic arrays) are cheap and powerful for catching endian/format mismatches early in the pipeline.
- Noisy warnings sometimes contain high-signal indicators; create a classification process to escalate warnings when they co-occur with quality anomalies.

Postmortem follow-up notes:
- We will run a one-week canary window where model-v2 is redeployed only after both normalized artifacts and enhanced runtime checks are in place. During this period, any float-cast warnings will trigger immediate rollback.
- SRE will create a retrospective write-up in the weekly SRE meeting (agenda item scheduled 2024-11-20).
- PR-879 (the serializer change) will be reverted in the build branch until the portable serializer is merged and covered by CI.

Appendices (quick artifacts and commands used during debugging):
- Quick float re-interpretation check used on host:
  python -c "import struct,sys; b=open('shard.bin','rb').read(16); print([struct.unpack('<f',b[i:i+4])[0] for i in range(0,16,4)])"
  python -c "import struct,sys; b=open('shard.bin','rb').read(16); print([struct.unpack('>f',b[i:i+4])[0] for i in range(0,16,4)])"
- Commands to detect builder correlation:
  git show --name-only PR-879
  aws s3 ls s3://redwood-artifacts/models/2024-11-14/ --recursive --human-readable
- Example log line that became useful:
  [2024-11-14T19:27:48Z] float_cast_warning: layer=tok_embed index=0 raw_exponent=255 interpreted_value=nan

Outstanding questions:
- Were there other artifacts produced by builder-3 in the prior 30 days that also used the new serializer? (Action: Artifact audit — eng-build).
- Should we implement a fail-closed policy for any artifact that lacks explicit schema metadata? (Action: Product + Security review).
